Beyond Fixed Acquisition Functions:
Temporal Difference Active Learning
for Perturbation Discovery

Xudong Zhang Affiliation: Center for Machine Learning Research, Peking University, Beijing, China Affiliation: AI for Science Institute (AISI), Beijing, China    Jianzhe Li Affiliation: Center for Machine Learning Research, Peking University, Beijing, China Affiliation: AI for Science Institute (AISI), Beijing, China    Yitong Tang Affiliation: Center for Machine Learning Research, Peking University, Beijing, China    Peijie Zhou Email: xudongzhang25@stu.pku.edu.cn*Equal contribution. †Corresponding author. Affiliation: Center for Machine Learning Research, Peking University, Beijing, China Affiliation: AI for Science Institute (AISI), Beijing, China Affiliation: Center for Quantitative Biology, Peking University, Beijing, China
Abstract

Genetic and drug perturbation screens are important tools for elucidating disease mechanisms and validating therapeutic targets, but experimental costs limit the number of candidates that can be tested. Existing perturbation screening methods typically update the surrogate model with feedback while keeping the acquisition function fixed, limiting their ability to adapt selection to different response landscapes. Experimental feedback reveals current hits and informs subsequent selection by updating candidate predictions, providing a training signal for learning how to select experiments. We formulate budgeted perturbation discovery as a sequential decision problem and propose Temporal Difference Active Learning (TDAL), which learns an acquisition function online through temporal difference learning from a single screening trajectory, accounting for current hits and future discoveries. TDAL uses the Hellinger distance between hit probabilities for unmeasured candidates before and after an experiment to weight successor value, and reuses measured outcomes through leave-batch-out (LBO) to construct virtual transitions and alleviate training data scarcity. Across eight public screens spanning single, double, and triple perturbations under varied experimental configurations, TDAL achieves an average rank of 1.63 among eleven methods and ranks first on four tasks, demonstrating its adaptability across response landscapes.

1  Introduction

Large-scale perturbational screens deepen the understanding of disease mechanisms and help validate therapeutic targets (Schmidt et al., 2022; Zhuang et al., 2019; Sanchez et al., 2021). The human genome comprises nearly 20,000 single-gene candidates, roughly 200 million pairs, and one trillion triples in terms of perturbation combinations. The costs of testing each perturbation and measuring its phenotype make exhaustive screening infeasible (Mehrjou et al., 2022; Pacchiano et al., 2023). Closed-loop systems have shown that model-guided experiment selection can improve biological discovery under limited resources (Xu et al., 2026; DeMeo et al., 2025). It is thus important to develop strategies that maximize cumulative discoveries within a fixed experimental budget.

Active learning addresses this challenge by iteratively fitting a surrogate model to measured outcomes and using an acquisition function to select subsequent experiments (Figure 1a). GeneDisco evaluates active learning methods for perturbation screening and reports substantial variation in their performance across experimental settings (Mehrjou et al., 2022). Existing methods employ different selection criteria to guide perturbation discovery. OAE (Pacchiano et al., 2023) seeks near-optimal perturbations, DiscoBAX (Lyle et al., 2023) considers response strength and mechanistic diversity, and Probability-of-Hit (PoH) (Rubbi et al., 2026) prioritizes perturbations that exceed a predefined phenotypic threshold. Recent approaches also incorporate language model agents or biological priors into experiment selection (Roohani et al., 2025; Hao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a).

Indeed, different response landscapes favor different selection strategies (Figure 1b). In conventional active learning, experimental feedback updates the surrogate model and changes subsequent selections, while the acquisition rule itself typically remains predefined. The same feedback can also inform how experiments should be selected: each experiment yields immediate discoveries and updates predictions for the remaining candidates, influencing future discovery opportunities. This motivates learning an acquisition function that accounts for both current and future discoveries from experimental feedback. We therefore formulate screening as a sequential decision problem and use experimental transitions to learn a dynamic acquisition function online (Figure 1a). However, unlike reinforcement learning with repeated episodes, a screening campaign follows a single trajectory that cannot be reset, with each candidate queried at most once and only one real transition generated per round. Learning an acquisition function from such limited feedback presents a particular challenge.

Here we introduce Temporal Difference Active Learning (TDAL), which learns a dynamic acquisition function online from experimental feedback to maximize cumulative discoveries. Building on surrogate hit probabilities, TDAL uses temporal difference learning to incorporate observed discoveries and feedback-weighted successor value into experiment selection. It weights successor value according to changes in predicted hit probabilities for the remaining candidates, reflecting how experimental feedback updates their predicted outcomes. To alleviate the scarcity of real transitions, TDAL constructs additional training transitions from previously measured outcomes through leave-batch-out (LBO). Our main contributions are threefold.

  • •

    We formulate perturbation discovery as a sequential decision problem and learn a dynamic acquisition function from experimental feedback to adapt to different response landscapes.

  • •

    We introduce TDAL, which learns online from a single screening trajectory through temporal difference learning. It uses the Hellinger distance to weight successor value and LBO to construct additional training transitions, alleviating training data scarcity.

  • •

    We evaluate TDAL across eight screens spanning single, double, and triple perturbations. TDAL ranks first on four tasks and achieves an average rank of 1.63 among eleven methods.

2  Related Work

2.1  Active Learning and Acquisition Function Learning

Active learning alternates between sample selection and model updates to improve predictions with fewer labels. Methods include BALD, which uses information gain (Houlsby et al., 2011), CoreSet, which emphasizes geometric coverage (Sener and Savarese, 2018), and BADGE, which combines uncertainty and diversity (Ash et al., 2020). For discovery, active search (Garnett et al., 2012), ENS (Jiang et al., 2017), and its batch extension (Jiang et al., 2018) evaluate future hits within the budget. IDS (Xu et al., 2022) balances instantaneous regret and information gain to increase cumulative response. These methods adapt sampling to observations but retain predefined acquisition functions.

Other approaches learn acquisition functions from data. Learning Active Learning predicts expected error reduction (Konyushkova et al., 2017). MetaBO trains acquisition functions through reinforcement learning across tasks (Volpp et al., 2020). Amortized active search trains a neural network to imitate ENS selections (Nguyen et al., 2024). In molecular discovery, GLARE updates its selection policy online using measured activity labels (Chen et al., 2025), while Zhang et al. (2026) learn a policy to identify the optimal molecule. SOFisher uses Double DQN to select spatial-omics fields of view (Li et al., 2026b). Our work focuses on perturbation screens, where TDAL learns a dynamic acquisition function online from experimental feedback.

2.2  Active Learning for Perturbation Discovery

Active learning guides the discovery of perturbations with target phenotypes under a limited experimental budget. GeneDisco provides a unified benchmark for gene perturbations (Mehrjou et al., 2022). OAE seeks near-optimal perturbations with high responses (Pacchiano et al., 2023), DiscoBAX balances response strength and mechanistic diversity (Lyle et al., 2023), and PoH selects candidates by their posterior probability of exceeding a predefined phenotypic threshold (Rubbi et al., 2026). RECOVER and NAIAD target drug and genetic combination discovery, respectively (Bertin et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2025), while BATCHIE uses information-driven batch design to improve predictions of drug combination responses (Tosh et al., 2025). These methods update surrogate models from observations while typically keeping acquisition functions fixed.

Biological priors and agents guide selection. IterPert improves predictions with multimodal priors (Huang et al., 2024), while BioBO combines gene representations and pathway information (Li et al., 2026a). Soper et al. (2025) and DeepAL (Zhu et al., 2026) combine knowledge graphs with Bayesian matrix factorization and representation learning, respectively, for double gene perturbation discovery. BioDiscoveryAgent and PerTurboAgent design perturbations using language models, experimental history, and tools (Roohani et al., 2025; Hao et al., 2025). AIDO.Builder updates models from feedback and reuses experience through memory (Guo et al., 2026). Gupta et al. (2025) found the tested agents insensitive to permuted feedback, whereas Wainrib et al. (2026) reported discovery gains from feedback beyond prior knowledge. We construct transitions from feedback to learn a dynamic acquisition function that adapts to different response landscapes (Appendix A.1).

3  Problem Formulation

We consider a fixed candidate pool and aim to maximize expected cumulative discoveries of perturbations that induce desired phenotypic responses within a fixed experimental budget. We formulate this task as a sequential decision problem and define an objective combining immediate discoveries with successor value weighted according to experimental feedback (notation in Appendix A.2).

3.1  Sequential Perturbation Discovery

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a finite pool of gene or gene combination perturbations. Testing a candidate x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} yields a scalar phenotype e⁡(x)e(x). We align effect directions across assays so that larger e⁡(x)e(x) indicates closer agreement with the target phenotype. For a threshold τ\tau fixed before screening, the hit indicator is z(x)=𝟏{e(x)≥τ}z(x)=\mathbf{1}\{e(x)\geq\tau\} (Rubbi et al., 2026). Let D0D_{0} contain the n0n_{0} candidate–phenotype pairs (x,e⁡(x))(x,e(x)) observed before sequential selection begins. The phenotypes of initially unmeasured candidates x∈U0x\in U_{0} are revealed only when queried. The subsequent screening process consists of TT rounds with batch size BB, subject to the experimental budget.

In the experimental loop shown in Figure 2, let AtA_{t} denote the selected batch at round t∈{0,…,T−1}t\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\} and Ot={(x,e⁡(x)):x∈At}O_{t}=\{(x,e(x)):x\in A_{t}\} its observed outcomes. Before selecting AtA_{t}, the available history is Ht=(D0,(Aj,Oj)0≤j<t)H_{t}=(D_{0},(A_{j},O_{j})_{0\leq j<t}). The measured dataset and unmeasured candidate pool are

Dt=D0∪⋃0≤j<tOj,Ut=𝒳∖{x:(x,e⁡(x))∈Dt}.D_{t}=D_{0}\cup\bigcup\nolimits_{0\leq j<t}O_{j},\qquad U_{t}=\mathcal{X}\setminus\{x:(x,e(x))\in D_{t}\}. (1)

A surrogate model trained on DtD_{t} estimates hit probabilities p^t​(x)\hat{p}_{t}(x) for x∈Utx\in U_{t}. The acquisition function selects At⊆UtA_{t}\subseteq U_{t} using the available history and surrogate predictions. Experimentally testing the selected batch yields OtO_{t} and a reward equal to the number of discoveries in round tt: Rt=∑x∈Atz⁡(x).R_{t}=\sum\nolimits_{x\in A_{t}}z(x). Appending (At,Ot)(A_{t},O_{t}) to the history gives Ht+1H_{t+1}, with Dt+1=Dt∪OtD_{t+1}=D_{t}\cup O_{t} and Ut+1=Ut∖AtU_{t+1}=U_{t}\setminus A_{t}. Each round thus produces a transition (Ht,At,Rt,Ht+1)(H_{t},A_{t},R_{t},H_{t+1}). After TT rounds, the final output consists of all verified hit candidates recorded in DTD_{T}, whose cumulative discovery count is CT=∑(x,e⁡(x))∈DTz⁡(x).C_{T}=\sum\nolimits_{(x,e(x))\in D_{T}}z(x).

3.2  Sequential Decision Objective

The screening goal is to maximize expected final discoveries 𝔼π​[CT∣H0]\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[C_{T}\mid H_{0}]. Each experiment yields the current discovery count and updates the surrogate model’s predictions for unmeasured candidates, informing estimates of future discovery value and selection in the next round. We use the current discovery count as the immediate reward and adjust the successor value weight according to prediction changes before and after the experiment, defining a surrogate learning objective weighted by experimental feedback. Let wt=w⁡(Ht,At,Ht+1)∈[0,1]w_{t}=w(H_{t},A_{t},H_{t+1})\in[0,1] denote the successor value weight determined by the observed transition. For a selection policy π\pi, define

Jw​(π)=𝔼π​[∑t=0T−1(∏j=0t−1wj)​Rt|H0].J_{w}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}\left(\prod\nolimits_{j=0}^{t-1}w_{j}\right)R_{t}\,\middle|\,H_{0}\right]. (2)

We seek a selection policy π\pi that maximizes Jw​(π)J_{w}(\pi). When wt=1w_{t}=1 for all tt, this is equivalent to maximizing expected final discoveries 𝔼π​[CT∣H0]\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[C_{T}\mid H_{0}].

To maximize JwJ_{w}, let Qt∗,w​(Ht,A)Q_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t},A) denote the expected weighted cumulative discoveries from round tt to T−1T-1, when batch AA is selected given history HtH_{t} and subsequent selections follow the optimal policy. This value combines current discoveries with weighted successor value through the Bellman equation for a finite horizon:

Qt∗,w(Ht,A)=𝔼[Rt+wtmaxA′⊆Ut+1Qt+1∗,w(Ht+1,A′)|Ht,At=A].Q_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t},A)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[R_{t}+w_{t}\max\nolimits_{A^{\prime}\subseteq U_{t+1}}Q_{t+1}^{*,w}(H_{t+1},A^{\prime})\,\middle|\,H_{t},A_{t}=A\right]. (3)

At each round, the optimal selection policy πw∗\pi_{w}^{*} selects the batch maximizing Qt∗,wQ_{t}^{*,w} given the current history, thereby maximizing the weighted cumulative discovery objective JwJ_{w}:

πw∗(Ht)∈argmaxA⊆UtQt∗,w(Ht,A),Jw(πw∗)=maxπJw(π)=maxA⊆U0Q0∗,w(H0,A).\displaystyle\pi_{w}^{*}(H_{t})\in\arg\max\nolimits_{A\subseteq U_{t}}Q_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t},A),J_{w}(\pi_{w}^{*})=\max\nolimits_{\pi}J_{w}(\pi)=\max\nolimits_{A\subseteq U_{0}}Q_{0}^{*,w}(H_{0},A). (4)

4  Temporal Difference Active Learning

Within this sequential decision framework, TDAL uses experimental feedback to update a dynamic acquisition function online through TD learning, accounting for current and future discoveries while adapting selection to different response landscapes (Figure 2). See Algorithm 1 (Appendix A.3).

4.1  Dynamic Acquisition Function

The optimal value Qt∗,w​(Ht,A)Q_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t},A) involves expectations over future experimental feedback and is difficult to compute directly. TDAL approximates this value using a dynamic acquisition function learned online from experimental feedback and built on surrogate predictions.

Surrogate model. In the active learning loop, the surrogate model approximates the posterior predictive distribution of unmeasured outcomes, providing a reference for estimating immediate discoveries. We use an MLP gβg_{\beta} with MC dropout and fit parameters βt\beta_{t} to data DtD_{t}. For each unmeasured candidate, we estimate p^t​(x)\hat{p}_{t}(x) as the proportion of sampled predictions at or above threshold τ\tau.

Value decomposition. Given the measured data DtD_{t}, R^t​(A)=∑x∈Ap^t​(x)\widehat{R}_{t}(A)=\sum_{x\in A}\hat{p}_{t}(x) estimates the number of discoveries in the unmeasured batch AA. Thus, the optimal batch value can be written as

Qt∗,w​(Ht,A)=R^t​(A)+𝔼[Rt−R^t(A)+wtmaxA′Qt+1∗,w(Ht+1,A′)|Ht,At=A]⏟Ft∗​(Ht,A).Q_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t},A)=\widehat{R}_{t}(A)+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\!\left[R_{t}-\widehat{R}_{t}(A)+w_{t}\max\nolimits_{A^{\prime}}Q_{t+1}^{*,w}(H_{t+1},A^{\prime})\,\middle|\,H_{t},A_{t}=A\right]}_{F_{t}^{*}(H_{t},A)}. (5)

The term Ft∗​(Ht,A)F_{t}^{*}(H_{t},A) accounts for the expected error in this estimate and the weighted value of subsequent discoveries. This decomposition allows value learning to build on the surrogate’s estimate of immediate discoveries, which provides a reference grounded in measured data.

Acquisition function parameterization. We approximate Ft∗​(Ht,A)F_{t}^{*}(H_{t},A) using the summed outputs Fθ​(st,A)F_{\theta}(s_{t},A) of a fully connected acquisition network fθf_{\theta}. The state sts_{t} summarizes screening progress, measured outcomes, and surrogate prediction statistics for unmeasured candidates. The candidate features ct​(x)c_{t}(x) combine a fixed biological representation with the surrogate model’s predictions. Adding each candidate’s network output to its estimated hit probability yields a dynamic acquisition function that scores candidates based on sts_{t} and ct​(x)c_{t}(x) (Appendices A.4–A.6)

qθ​(st,x)=p^t​(x)+fθ​(st,ct​(x)).q_{\theta}(s_{t},x)=\hat{p}_{t}(x)+f_{\theta}(s_{t},c_{t}(x)). (6)

We use an additive approximation QθQ_{\theta} to make batch maximization tractable. Selecting the BB unmeasured candidates with the highest scores maximizes

Qθ​(st,A)=∑x∈Aqθ​(st,x)≈Qt∗,w​(Ht,A).Q_{\theta}(s_{t},A)=\sum\nolimits_{x\in A}q_{\theta}(s_{t},x)\approx Q_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t},A). (7)

4.2  Temporal Difference Learning

We train the acquisition network fθf_{\theta} using real and LBO transitions (Appendix A.7). Each transition provides an observed discovery count and a successor state, supplying a learning signal for the acquisition function to adapt its selection strategy to different response landscapes.

Real transitions. After querying batch AtA_{t}, we obtain observations OtO_{t} and discovery count RtR_{t}. We refit the surrogate on Dt+1D_{t+1} and construct the successor selection state st+1s_{t+1}. With successor value weight wtw_{t}, the round is stored as the training record ξt=(st,At,Rt,wt,st+1).\xi_{t}=(s_{t},A_{t},R_{t},w_{t},s_{t+1}).

Virtual transitions through LBO. Screening follows a single trajectory, which cannot be reset to test alternative selection sequences within the same budget. Each round therefore provides only one real batch transition. LBO supplements these transitions by temporarily hiding measured outcomes and then restoring them to reconstruct experimental feedback. Let D+D^{+} and U+U^{+} denote the current measured dataset and unmeasured pool. For a batch AA of measured candidates, hiding its outcomes gives D−=D+∖{(x,e⁡(x)):x∈A}.D^{-}=D^{+}\setminus\{(x,e(x)):x\in A\}. We refit the surrogate model on D−D^{-} to construct the predecessor state s−s^{-}, and construct the successor state s+s^{+} from D+D^{+} with the outcomes restored. The discovery count RR is computed from the batch’s observed outcomes. We compute ww by comparing hit probability estimates before and after restoration over U+U^{+}. The resulting virtual transition is ξ~=(s−,A,R,w,s+)\widetilde{\xi}=(s^{-},A,R,w,s^{+}). Real and virtual transitions enter the same replay buffer ℛ\mathcal{R}, providing more training data without additional experiments.

Feedback weights. For each candidate, hit and nonhit probabilities define a Bernoulli distribution. For both real and virtual transitions, we use Hellinger distance (Hellinger, 1909) to compare these distributions before and after feedback over the remaining pool. Unchanged predictions across Ut+1U_{t+1} give wt=0w_{t}=0, while larger Hellinger distances assign more weight to successor value:

wt2=∑x∈Ut+1HBer2​(p^t​(x),p^t+1​(x))|Ut+1|,HBer2​(p,q)=1−p​q−(1−p)​(1−q).w_{t}^{2}=\frac{\sum\nolimits_{x\in U_{t+1}}H_{\mathrm{Ber}}^{2}(\hat{p}_{t}(x),\hat{p}_{t+1}(x))}{|U_{t+1}|},\qquad H_{\mathrm{Ber}}^{2}(p,q)=1-\sqrt{pq}-\sqrt{(1-p)(1-q)}. (8)

Updating the acquisition function through TD learning. For a replay transition ξ=(s,A,R,w,s′)\xi=(s,A,R,w,s^{\prime}), we follow Double DQN. The current acquisition function selects the successor batch Aθ′A^{\prime}_{\theta}, and the target network evaluates its batch value Qθ¯​(s′,Aθ′)Q_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime},A^{\prime}_{\theta}) (van Hasselt et al., 2016). Here, θ¯\bar{\theta} denotes the target network parameters. The current discovery count and successor value weighted by ww form the TD target YY. Both real and LBO transitions use this target. During each update, the stored surrogate predictions remain fixed, and we optimize only θ\theta.

Y=R+w​Qθ¯​(s′,Aθ′),ℒTD​(θ)=𝔼ξ∼ℛ​[Huber⁡(Qθ​(s,A)−Y)].Y=R+wQ_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime},A^{\prime}_{\theta}),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{R}}\left[\operatorname{Huber}\!\left(Q_{\theta}(s,A)-Y\right)\right]. (9)

4.3  Theoretical Analysis

We analyze weighted Bellman optimality, predictive improvement, and the final discovery gap.

Proposition 1 (Weighted Bellman optimality). For a finite horizon, let Qt∗,wQ_{t}^{*,w} satisfy the Bellman recursion in equation 3, and let πw∗\pi_{w}^{*} select a feasible batch maximizing Qt∗,w​(Ht,A)Q_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t},A) at every reachable history. Then Jw​(πw∗)=maxπ⁡Jw​(π)J_{w}(\pi_{w}^{*})=\max\nolimits_{\pi}J_{w}(\pi). Thus, optimal batch selection maximizes the weighted discovery objective (Appendix B.1).

Proposition 2 (Feedback and predictive improvement). Fix Ht,AtH_{t},A_{t} and U=Ut+1U=U_{t+1}, with |U|>0|U|>0. Let px=Pr⁡(z⁡(x)=1∣Ht,At)p_{x}=\Pr(z(x)=1\mid H_{t},A_{t}) and qx=Pr⁡(z⁡(x)=1∣Ht,At,Ot)q_{x}=\Pr(z(x)=1\mid H_{t},A_{t},O_{t}) denote hit probabilities before and after feedback. Let Δpred\Delta_{\mathrm{pred}} denote the expected decrease in squared loss from (px−z⁡(x))2(p_{x}-z(x))^{2} to (qx−z⁡(x))2(q_{x}-z(x))^{2}, averaged over x∈Ux\in U (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). With wtw_{t} computed from these probabilities, the expected predictive improvement conditional on Ht,AtH_{t},A_{t} satisfies

𝔼⁡[wt4]≤Δpred=1|U|​∑x∈U𝔼⁡[(qx−px)2]≤2​𝔼​[wt2].\mathbb{E}[w_{t}^{4}]\leq\Delta_{\mathrm{pred}}=\frac{1}{|U|}\sum\nolimits_{x\in U}\mathbb{E}[(q_{x}-p_{x})^{2}]\leq 2\mathbb{E}[w_{t}^{2}]. (10)

This bounds predictive improvement using the Hellinger weight. For a query aa revealing only z⁡(a)z(a), let r=Pr⁡(z⁡(a)=1)∈(0,1)r=\Pr(z(a)=1)\in(0,1), px+=Pr⁡(z⁡(x)=1∣z⁡(a)=1)p_{x}^{+}=\Pr(z(x)=1\mid z(a)=1), and px−=Pr⁡(z⁡(x)=1∣z⁡(a)=0)p_{x}^{-}=\Pr(z(x)=1\mid z(a)=0), suppressing the same conditioning. The predictive improvement decomposes as

Δpred​(a)=r⁡(1−r)|U|​∑x∈U(px+−px−)2.\Delta_{\mathrm{pred}}(a)=\frac{r(1-r)}{|U|}\sum\nolimits_{x\in U}(p_{x}^{+}-p_{x}^{-})^{2}. (11)

Outcome uncertainty r⁡(1−r)r(1-r) multiplies the mean squared difference between remaining predictions under the two outcomes. Queries without hits can therefore inform selection (Appendix B.2).

Proposition 3 (Final discovery gap). Under the same initial information and budget, let πC∗\pi_{C}^{*} maximize expected final discoveries and let πθ\pi_{\theta} select a feasible batch maximizing Qθ​(st,A)Q_{\theta}(s_{t},A) at each round. For feedback weights wt∈[0,1]w_{t}\in[0,1], write Wt=∏j=0t−1wjW_{t}=\prod\nolimits_{j=0}^{t-1}w_{j}, with W0=1W_{0}=1. Define the value error over feasible batches as εtw​(Ht)=maxA⁡|Qθ​(st,A)−Qt∗,w​(Ht,A)|\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H_{t})=\max\nolimits_{A}|Q_{\theta}(s_{t},A)-Q_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t},A)| and the objective weighting bias as ΔC​(w)=𝔼πC∗​[∑t=0T−1(1−Wt)​Rt∣H0]\Delta_{C}(w)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{C}^{*}}[\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}(1-W_{t})R_{t}\mid H_{0}]. The final discovery gap satisfies

𝔼πC∗​[CT∣H0]−𝔼πθ​[CT∣H0]≤ΔC​(w)+2​𝔼πθ​[∑t=0T−1Wt​εtw​(Ht)∣H0].\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{C}^{*}}[C_{T}\mid H_{0}]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[C_{T}\mid H_{0}]\leq\Delta_{C}(w)+2\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}W_{t}\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H_{t})\mid H_{0}\right]. (12)

The first term measures discovery return attenuated by weighting. The second bounds selection losses from value estimation error. Small terms imply near-optimal expected final discoveries. For constant weights under a common value error bound, smaller weights lower the error bound but raise the bias bound. Larger weights lower the bias bound but raise the error bound (Appendix B.3).

5  Experiments and Results

We evaluate hit discovery performance across eight public genetic perturbation datasets under fixed experimental budgets. Then we examine how local landscape structure affects active discovery, assess individual components through ablations, and analyze candidate rankings over selection rounds.

5.1  Experimental Setup

Data and budgets. We evaluate TDAL on eight public datasets recording phenotypic responses to genetic perturbations, aiming to identify perturbations producing desired phenotypic changes (Appendix C.1). These comprise four single perturbation tasks (Schmidt et al., 2022; Zhuang et al., 2019; Carnevale et al., 2022), three double perturbation tasks (Fong et al., 2025; Simpson et al., 2023; Horlbeck et al., 2018), and one triple perturbation task (Kuzmin et al., 2020), with candidate pools ranging from 11,067 to 214,642. Initial sample sizes, batch sizes, and budgets vary across tasks (Table C2).

Experimental protocol. We conduct retrospective sequential evaluation using measured phenotypes from these genetic perturbation datasets. Candidate identities and fixed representations are available at the start. Each method initially receives the phenotypes of n0n_{0} candidates, and the remaining outcomes are revealed as candidates are selected in subsequent rounds. We fix the hit threshold τ\tau before screening to target the top 5% of candidates in the predefined effect direction (Mehrjou et al., 2022). Selection aims to maximize final cumulative hits CTC_{T} within the budget, and recall RecallT=CT/∑x∈𝒳z⁡(x)\operatorname{Recall}_{T}=C_{T}/\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}z(x) measures discovery coverage. Within each of five seeds (0–4), methods share the candidate pool, initial data, budget, and hit threshold (Appendix C.2).

Baselines. We compare diverse baselines with publicly available implementations (Appendix C.3). Perturbation discovery baselines include PoH (Rubbi et al., 2026), OAE (Pacchiano et al., 2023), and DiscoBAX (Lyle et al., 2023). General acquisition functions include UCB (Srinivas et al., 2010), Expected Improvement (Jones et al., 1998), and Thompson Sampling (Thompson, 1933). Active learning baselines include BADGE (Ash et al., 2020), CoreSet (Sener and Savarese, 2018), and TopUncertain and KMeans-Embedding from GeneDisco (Mehrjou et al., 2022). Random serves as a control. For computational scalability, we evaluate DiscoBAX on four single perturbation tasks.

5.2  Budgeted Perturbation Discovery

Single perturbations. Across five seeds, TDAL achieves the highest mean final discovery counts on IFN-γ\gamma, IL-2, and Carnevale (Figure 3a–d). Final cumulative hit counts are 270.6±6.1270.6\pm 6.1, 367.4±3.0367.4\pm 3.0, and 161.2±8.6161.2\pm 8.6, corresponding to recalls of 31.00%, 42.08%, and 18.40%, respectively. On NK, CoreSet, TDAL, and Random reach recalls of 13.01%, 12.49%, and 11.71%, respectively, with small gaps between active methods and Random. TDAL shows strong performance and adaptability across single gene perturbation landscapes.

Combinatorial perturbations. TDAL ranks first on Kuzmin and third on SCHEMATIC, with final recalls of 38.59% and 29.01%, respectively (Figure 3e–h). Although ranked second on Simpson K562 and Horlbeck Jurkat, TDAL approaches complete hit recovery with recalls of 94.40% and 99.45%, respectively, within 0.2 percentage points of the best method. These results show consistently strong performance across double and triple gene perturbation tasks.

Stability across tasks. Fixed acquisition functions favor different response landscapes (Mehrjou et al., 2022). Among eleven methods evaluated on all eight main tasks, TDAL achieves an average rank of 1.63, placing first on four tasks, second on three, and third on one (Figure 3i). TDAL’s top three performance on every task supports its adaptability across response landscapes (Appendix D).

5.3  Landscape Structure and Active Discovery

Real landscapes. Active learning gains over Random vary across datasets, with several methods underperforming Random on NK (Figure 3). We examine local hit structure in the fixed candidate representations. Within an analysis sample, enrichment is the mean hit rate among each hit candidate’s 10 nearest neighbors divided by the sample’s overall hit rate. Across eight tasks, enrichment ranges from 0.83×0.83\times to 6.27×6.27\times. The gray dashed fit to mean gains across nine shared baselines (Figure 4a) indicates that stronger local hit clustering is associated with greater active learning gains.

Controlled landscapes. To further examine this relationship, we construct simulated landscapes with controlled spatial structure. We keep the positions of 17,660 candidates and the set of phenotype values fixed, changing their assignment so that hits become progressively more clustered. With nearly random hit locations, methods perform close to Random. Across five enrichment levels, stronger clustering yields larger gains for TDAL and several baselines, although the benefit varies across acquisition functions (Figure 4b). These results indicate that local hit structure can provide useful information for active selection. Construction details and results are in Appendix E.

5.4  Component Ablations

Dynamic acquisition function. Surrogate only removes fθf_{\theta} and selects solely by p^t​(x)\hat{p}_{t}(x), updating the surrogate model while keeping the acquisition function fixed (Appendix C.3). Its mean final discovery counts are lower than full TDAL on all four tasks, supporting learning the acquisition function alongside surrogate updates. w/o successor retains fθf_{\theta} but sets wt=0w_{t}=0, fitting the residual Rt−R^t​(At)R_{t}-\smash[t]{\widehat{R}}_{t}(A_{t}) between observed and surrogate estimated discoveries. Its mean final discovery count exceeds Surrogate only on all four tasks, showing that current feedback alone can train a dynamic acquisition function. Full TDAL adds further gains on every task, indicating that incorporating estimated future discovery value improves selection beyond learning from current feedback alone.

Training and scoring design. Fixing wt=1w_{t}=1 lowers mean final discovery counts below both full TDAL and w/o successor on all four tasks. Undiscounted successor value can therefore impair selection, supporting adjustment of its weight to experimental feedback. Removing LBO also lowers mean final discoveries on every task, supporting the use of additional reconstructed transitions to train QθQ_{\theta} when real experimental feedback is sparse. w/o anchor removes the explicit p^t​(x)\hat{p}_{t}(x) from the score while retaining surrogate predictions in the inputs. Its final mean decreases on the two 60-round single perturbation tasks but increases slightly on the two 200-round tasks. With more rounds of online training, the acquisition function maintains performance without the explicit probability baseline. Detailed ablation settings are provided in Appendix F.

5.5  Online Feedback and Selection Paths

To examine how online learning changes candidate selection, we analyze 85 IL-2 hits discovered in all five TDAL runs but in none of the Surrogate only runs. Discoveries concentrate in the second half of screening, with the median cumulative count rising from 16 after 30 rounds to 85 at completion (Figure 5a). Candidate ranks under TDAL progressively improve before selection (Figure 5b). Across the 85 candidates, their mean ranks at selection are 16.6 under TDAL and 9,780 under concurrent surrogate predictions, showing how accumulated feedback helps prioritize hits ranked poorly by the surrogate alone (Appendix Figure F1).

6  Conclusion

We introduce TDAL to learn a dynamic acquisition function online from a single perturbation screening trajectory. Building on surrogate-estimated hit probabilities, TDAL uses temporal difference learning to incorporate observed discoveries and feedback-weighted successor value, while LBO reconstructs additional training transitions from measured outcomes. By learning how to select experiments from feedback accumulated within the ongoing screen, TDAL adapts candidate selection to both immediate discoveries and subsequent discovery opportunities under limited experimental feedback. Across eight public screens spanning single, double, and triple perturbations, TDAL achieves an average rank of 1.63 among eleven methods, demonstrating consistent discovery performance across diverse response landscapes.

Limitations. Our evaluation is retrospective, and the additive acquisition function does not explicitly model interactions among candidates within a batch. Feedback weighting also relies on surrogate-estimated hit probabilities, motivating further investigation of its robustness to prediction errors. Future work will explore batch-aware selection and alternative feedback weighting strategies, alongside prospective validation in closed-loop biological experiments.

Reproducibility statement

The TDAL implementation, task configurations, and data preparation scripts are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TDAL/, with data sources and running instructions. Appendices A–C provide implementation details, theoretical assumptions and proofs, and experimental settings, respectively.

AI use statement

The research ideas and methodological design originated from the authors. Generative AI tools were used to assist with code development, checking mathematical derivations and proofs, and improving manuscript clarity and grammar. The authors reviewed and verified all AI-assisted content and take full responsibility for the final work.
