Appendix

Appendix A Algorithm and Implementation Details

A.1  Comparison with Related Methods

Table A1 compares representative methods for perturbation screening, molecular virtual screening, and spatial omics sampling across five mechanisms including surrogate updates, biological knowledge, online acquisition updates, value bootstrapping, and experience augmentation.

Surrogate updates use newly measured outcomes to fit a model that predicts unmeasured phenotypes or activities. Biological knowledge guides selection through pathway information, literature, or knowledge encoded in language models. BioBO and PerTurboAgent combine such knowledge with response modeling, whereas BioDiscoveryAgent incorporates experimental observations into its language model context without fitting a response surrogate. SOFisher uses observed spatial features as inputs to its sampling policy rather than fitting a phenotype prediction model.

Online acquisition updates use feedback from the current task to update the acquisition function’s parameters. Value bootstrapping constructs training targets from current rewards and estimated successor values. GLARE updates its selection policy during screening but does not explicitly bootstrap a successor value. SOFisher trains its sampling policy through value bootstrapping before application and uses fixed policy parameters on new tissue sections, while incorporating newly sampled observations into the state. TDAL performs both acquisition updates and successor value bootstrapping within the current screening task.

Experience augmentation reconstructs additional transitions from measured outcomes to train the acquisition function. In budgeted experimental design without replacement, the measured dataset grows while the unmeasured pool and remaining budget shrink. A screen therefore provides a single executed trajectory and cannot return to an earlier state to test alternative experimental sequences within the same budget. LBO reconstructs predecessor states in which a measured batch has not yet been observed, then restores that batch’s real outcomes to form additional transitions to a known successor state. The same experimental outcomes can thus support batch value learning under different information states, expanding online training experience without additional experiments.

A.2  Notation

Table A2 summarizes the main notation used in the problem formulation and TDAL.

A.3  Complete TDAL Algorithm

Algorithm 1 summarizes TDAL from initialization through the end of screening. Starting from the initial observations D0D_{0}, TDAL fits a surrogate model, estimates hit probabilities for candidates in the initial unmeasured pool U0U_{0}, and forms the initial selection state. It then constructs initial LBO transitions from D0D_{0} to initialize the acquisition network through TD training before the first query.

At each round, the acquisition function scores candidates in UtU_{t}, and TDAL queries the BB candidates with the highest scores. The observed outcomes are added to DtD_{t}, and the queried candidates are removed from UtU_{t}. TDAL refits the surrogate model on the updated data. Before the next round, it updates predictions over Ut+1U_{t+1} to construct the successor state. Comparing hit probabilities before and after the experiment over this pool gives the Hellinger weight. The selected batch, observed discovery count, feedback weight, and current and successor states form a real transition. Real and online LBO transitions enter the replay buffer, from which TD updates train the acquisition network for subsequent selection. After TT rounds, TDAL returns all verified hit candidates.

A.4  Candidate Representations

The mapping ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) encodes candidate perturbation xx as a vector of fixed dimension, providing gene functional information to the surrogate and acquisition network.

Human tasks use genome-wide CRISPR–Cas9 knockout screening data from the Broad Institute’s Project Achilles. The CERES gene dependency profiles in DepMap 20Q4 provide 808-dimensional gene representations. Each dimension corresponds to a cancer cell line and describes the effect of knocking out the gene on cell growth. CERES corrects for copy number effects (Meyers et al., 2017). The Kuzmin yeast task uses the 500-dimensional STRING network embeddings released with Mashup (Cho et al., 2016). These base gene representations remain fixed during screening. For a single gene perturbation, ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) is the corresponding gene embedding.

For a candidate xx containing m∈{2,3}m\in\{2,3\} genes with embeddings 𝐯1,…,𝐯m\mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{m}, we define

ϕ⁡(x)=[1m​∑i=1m𝐯i,2m⁡(m−1)​∑i<j|𝐯i−𝐯j|,2m⁡(m−1)​∑i<j𝐯i⊙𝐯j].\phi(x)=\left[\frac{1}{m}\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{v}_{i},\,\frac{2}{m(m-1)}\sum\nolimits_{i<j}|\mathbf{v}_{i}-\mathbf{v}_{j}|,\,\frac{2}{m(m-1)}\sum\nolimits_{i<j}\mathbf{v}_{i}\odot\mathbf{v}_{j}\right]. (13)

The brackets concatenate the mean embedding, mean elementwise absolute difference, and mean elementwise product, with ⊙\odot denoting elementwise multiplication. Averaging over all members and unordered pairs makes this construction invariant to gene order.

A.5  Surrogate Model and Hit Probability Estimation

Model and training. The surrogate takes a fixed vector representation (embedding) ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) of candidate perturbation xx as input and predicts the phenotype e⁡(x)e(x) after aligning the effect direction. Its two hidden layers have widths 128 and 64. Each applies a linear transformation followed by ReLU and dropout. A final linear layer produces a scalar output. The model is

𝐡sur(1)​(x)\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{sur}}^{(1)}(x) =Dropout0.2⁡(ReLU⁡(W1sur​ϕ​(x)+b1sur))∈ℝ128,\displaystyle=\operatorname{Dropout}_{0.2}\!\left(\operatorname{ReLU}(W_{1}^{\mathrm{sur}}\phi(x)+b_{1}^{\mathrm{sur}})\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{128}, (14)
𝐡sur(2)​(x)\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{sur}}^{(2)}(x) =Dropout0.2⁡(ReLU⁡(W2sur​𝐡sur(1)​(x)+b2sur))∈ℝ64,\displaystyle=\operatorname{Dropout}_{0.2}\!\left(\operatorname{ReLU}(W_{2}^{\mathrm{sur}}\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{sur}}^{(1)}(x)+b_{2}^{\mathrm{sur}})\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{64},
gβ​(ϕ​(x))\displaystyle g_{\beta}(\phi(x)) =Woutsur​𝐡sur(2)​(x)+boutsur∈ℝ.\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{out}}^{\mathrm{sur}}\mathbf{h}_{\mathrm{sur}}^{(2)}(x)+b_{\mathrm{out}}^{\mathrm{sur}}\in\mathbb{R}.

Here, Dropout0.2\operatorname{Dropout}_{0.2} denotes dropout with probability 0.2, and β\beta contains all weights and biases of the hidden and output layers. Predictive uncertainty is estimated through MC dropout (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016).

At each round, the measured data DtD_{t} are split into a training set DttrD_{t}^{\mathrm{tr}} and a validation set DtvalD_{t}^{\mathrm{val}} for early stopping, and the model parameters are reinitialized. The surrogate fits measured phenotypes by minimizing the mean squared error

ℒsur​(β)=1|Dttr|​∑(x,e⁡(x))∈Dttr(gβ​(ϕ⁡(x))−e⁡(x))2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sur}}(\beta)=\frac{1}{|D_{t}^{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{(x,e(x))\in D_{t}^{\mathrm{tr}}}\bigl(g_{\beta}(\phi(x))-e(x)\bigr)^{2}. (15)

Dropout is active during training and disabled when evaluating validation mean squared error after each epoch. Let βt(j)\beta_{t}^{(j)} denote the parameters after epoch jj, and let JtJ_{t} be the number of epochs completed in the current round. We select the final model by minimizing validation error,

jt∗\displaystyle j_{t}^{*} =arg⁡min1≤j≤Jt​1|Dtval|​∑(x,e⁡(x))∈Dtval(gβt(j)​(ϕ⁡(x))−e⁡(x))2,\displaystyle=\arg\min_{1\leq j\leq J_{t}}\frac{1}{|D_{t}^{\mathrm{val}}|}\sum_{(x,e(x))\in D_{t}^{\mathrm{val}}}\bigl(g_{\beta_{t}^{(j)}}(\phi(x))-e(x)\bigr)^{2}, (16)
βt\displaystyle\beta_{t} =βt(jt∗).\displaystyle=\beta_{t}^{(j_{t}^{*})}.

Predictive statistics. Dropout remains active at inference. For each unmeasured candidate x∈Utx\in U_{t}, we independently sample KK forward passes. Denote the kkth stochastic forward pass by gβt(k)g_{\beta_{t}}^{(k)}, giving the phenotype prediction e^t(k)​(x)=gβt(k)​(ϕ⁡(x))\widehat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(x)=g_{\beta_{t}}^{(k)}(\phi(x)). The predictive mean, uncertainty, and hit probability are estimated by the sample mean, standard deviation, and fraction reaching the hit threshold, respectively,

μ^t​(x)\displaystyle\widehat{\mu}_{t}(x) =1K​∑k=1Ke^t(k)​(x),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(x), (17)
σ^t​(x)\displaystyle\widehat{\sigma}_{t}(x) =[1K​∑k=1K(e^t(k)​(x)−μ^t​(x))2]1/2,\displaystyle=\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\widehat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(x)-\widehat{\mu}_{t}(x)\bigr)^{2}\right]^{1/2},
p^t​(x)\displaystyle\hat{p}_{t}(x) =1K∑k=1K𝟏{e^t(k)(x)≥τ}.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(x)\geq\tau\}.

These statistics define candidate features and the selection state. The hit probability also provides the acquisition function’s base score and is used to compute the Hellinger weight.

A.6  State Representation and Acquisition Function Parameterization

Dynamic candidate features. For each unmeasured candidate x∈Utx\in U_{t}, the acquisition network receives the shared selection state sts_{t} and candidate features ct​(x)c_{t}(x). These features combine the fixed biological representation ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) with the surrogate model’s predicted mean, uncertainty, and hit probability. We center the mean at the hit threshold and scale both the mean and uncertainty, giving

ct​(x)=[ϕ⁡(x),μ^t​(x)−τat,log⁡(1+σ^t​(x)at),p^t​(x)].c_{t}(x)=\left[\phi(x),\,\frac{\widehat{\mu}_{t}(x)-\tau}{a_{t}},\,\log\!\left(1+\frac{\widehat{\sigma}_{t}(x)}{a_{t}}\right),\,\hat{p}_{t}(x)\right]. (18)

Here, μ^t​(x)\widehat{\mu}_{t}(x) and σ^t​(x)\widehat{\sigma}_{t}(x) are the predictive mean and standard deviation defined in Appendix A.5. The hit probability p^t​(x)\hat{p}_{t}(x) is included without rescaling.

The normalization denominator ata_{t} is computed from the phenotypes already measured in DtD_{t}. It is the larger of their interquartile range (75th minus 25th percentile) and population standard deviation, with a minimum of 10−610^{-6} to prevent division by zero. The same denominator is used for all candidates scored at that round. Their predicted means and uncertainties remain specific to each candidate. We recompute ata_{t} when the measured data change.

Selection state. The selection state sts_{t} is a vector summary of the current screening history HtH_{t} that provides global information for the dynamic acquisition function. Shared by all candidates, it combines screening progress, measured outcomes, and surrogate prediction statistics over the unmeasured pool UtU_{t}. Its 15 components follow the network input order

st=[\displaystyle s_{t}=\Big[ |Dt|M,M−|Dt|M,⌈min⁡{M−|Dt|,|Ut|}/B⌉⌈M/B⌉,|Ut||𝒳|,min⁡{B,M−|Dt|,|Ut|}B,\displaystyle\frac{|D_{t}|}{M},\,\frac{M-|D_{t}|}{M},\,\frac{\lceil\min\{M-|D_{t}|,|U_{t}|\}/B\rceil}{\lceil M/B\rceil},\,\frac{|U_{t}|}{|\mathcal{X}|},\,\frac{\min\{B,M-|D_{t}|,|U_{t}|\}}{B}, (19)
τ,max(x,e⁡(x))∈Dt⁡e⁡(x),at,MeanUt⁡(p^t),SDUt⁡(p^t),P90,Ut⁡(p^t),\displaystyle\tau,\,\max\nolimits_{(x,e(x))\in D_{t}}e(x),\,a_{t},\,\operatorname{Mean}_{U_{t}}(\hat{p}_{t}),\,\operatorname{SD}_{U_{t}}(\hat{p}_{t}),\,\operatorname{P}_{90,U_{t}}(\hat{p}_{t}),
MeanUt⁡(μ^t−τat),SDUt⁡(μ^t−τat),\displaystyle\operatorname{Mean}_{U_{t}}\!\left(\frac{\widehat{\mu}_{t}-\tau}{a_{t}}\right),\,\operatorname{SD}_{U_{t}}\!\left(\frac{\widehat{\mu}_{t}-\tau}{a_{t}}\right),
OPENMeanUt⁡(σ^tat),P90,Ut⁡(σ^tat)]∈ℝ15.\displaystyle\operatorname{Mean}_{U_{t}}\!\left(\frac{\widehat{\sigma}_{t}}{a_{t}}\right),\,\operatorname{P}_{90,U_{t}}\!\left(\frac{\widehat{\sigma}_{t}}{a_{t}}\right)\Big]\in\mathbb{R}^{15}.

Here, MeanUt\operatorname{Mean}_{U_{t}}, SDUt\operatorname{SD}_{U_{t}}, and P90,Ut\operatorname{P}_{90,U_{t}} denote the mean, population standard deviation, and 90th percentile over candidates x∈Utx\in U_{t}. The first five components describe the measured budget fraction, remaining budget fraction, normalized remaining rounds, remaining pool fraction, and query batch size relative to BB. These ratios are clipped to [0,1][0,1]. The batch size ratio is one for the full batches used here.

The hit threshold τ\tau, largest measured phenotype max(x,e⁡(x))∈Dt⁡e⁡(x)\max\nolimits_{(x,e(x))\in D_{t}}e(x), and normalization denominator ata_{t} retain the phenotype scale after aligning the effect direction. Statistics of the hit probability p^t​(x)\hat{p}_{t}(x), normalized predicted effect (μ^t​(x)−τ)/at(\widehat{\mu}_{t}(x)-\tau)/a_{t}, and scaled uncertainty σ^t​(x)/at\widehat{\sigma}_{t}(x)/a_{t} summarize predictions over x∈Utx\in U_{t}. The uncertainty statistics use the scaled standard deviation.

Acquisition network. The acquisition network fθf_{\theta} is the trainable component of qθ=p^t+fθq_{\theta}=\hat{p}_{t}+f_{\theta}. For each unmeasured candidate x∈Utx\in U_{t}, its encoding and network layers are

uθ​(x)\displaystyle u_{\theta}(x) =ReLU⁡(Wenc​ϕ⁡(x)max⁡{‖ϕ⁡(x)‖2,10−8}+benc)∈ℝ64,\displaystyle=\operatorname{ReLU}\!\left(W_{\mathrm{enc}}\frac{\phi(x)}{\max\{\|\phi(x)\|_{2},10^{-8}\}}+b_{\mathrm{enc}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{64}, (20)
𝐡t(0)​(x)\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(0)}(x) =[st,uθ​(x),μ^t​(x)−τat,log⁡(1+σ^t​(x)at),p^t​(x)]∈ℝ82,\displaystyle=\left[s_{t},\,u_{\theta}(x),\,\frac{\widehat{\mu}_{t}(x)-\tau}{a_{t}},\,\log\!\left(1+\frac{\widehat{\sigma}_{t}(x)}{a_{t}}\right),\,\hat{p}_{t}(x)\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{82},
𝐡t(k)​(x)\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(k)}(x) =ReLU(Wkacq𝐡t(k−1)(x)+bkacq)∈ℝ128,k=1,2,\displaystyle=\operatorname{ReLU}\!\left(W_{k}^{\mathrm{acq}}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(k-1)}(x)+b_{k}^{\mathrm{acq}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{128},\quad k=1,2,
fθ​(st,ct​(x))\displaystyle f_{\theta}(s_{t},c_{t}(x)) =Woutacq​𝐡t(2)​(x)+boutacq∈ℝ.\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{out}}^{\mathrm{acq}}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(2)}(x)+b_{\mathrm{out}}^{\mathrm{acq}}\in\mathbb{R}.

Here, uθ​(x)u_{\theta}(x) encodes the normalized fixed representation. The input 𝐡t(0)​(x)\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(0)}(x) concatenates the 15 state features, 64 encoding features, and three surrogate prediction features from ct​(x)c_{t}(x).

The parameters θ\theta include the weights and biases of the projection, two hidden layers, and output layer. The static embeddings remain fixed, while the projection is learned with the acquisition network. The output layer’s weights and bias are initialized to zero, so that fθ=0f_{\theta}=0 and qθ=p^tq_{\theta}=\hat{p}_{t} before initial TD training.

A.7  TD Learning and Experience Replay

LBO transition construction. Initial LBO hides batches from D0D_{0} to train the acquisition network before the first query. Online LBO draws hidden batches from candidates measured after initialization, so a batch can combine observations from different rounds. Algorithm 2 gives the construction for both stages.

The current measured dataset D+D^{+} and unmeasured pool U+U^{+} define the successor state s+s^{+}. Each hidden batch produces a different predecessor state, but restoring its outcomes returns to this same successor state. For a nonterminal successor, let p^+​(x)\hat{p}^{+}(x) denote the MC dropout hit probability estimated by the surrogate trained on D+D^{+}, for x∈U+x\in U^{+}. For initial LBO, the successor dataset is D+=D0D^{+}=D_{0}, giving p^+​(x)=p^0​(x)\hat{p}^{+}(x)=\hat{p}_{0}(x). For online LBO after round tt, it is D+=Dt+1D^{+}=D_{t+1}, giving p^+​(x)=p^t+1​(x)\hat{p}^{+}(x)=\hat{p}_{t+1}(x).

For each hidden batch AA, removing its outcomes from D+D^{+} gives the predecessor dataset D−D^{-}, and returning its candidates to the unmeasured pool gives U−U^{-}. We fit the predecessor surrogate gβ−g_{\beta^{-}} to D−D^{-} with validation early stopping. Its MC dropout predictions give predecessor hit probabilities p^−​(x)\hat{p}^{-}(x) for x∈U−x\in U^{-}. These predictions also define s−s^{-} and the candidate features, with the phenotype scale and screening progress recomputed from D−D^{-}. The Hellinger weight compares p^−​(x)\hat{p}^{-}(x) and p^+​(x)\hat{p}^{+}(x) over the shared remaining pool U+⊆U−U^{+}\subseteq U^{-}. The observed discoveries in AA give the transition reward RR. The predecessor state, hidden batch, reward, weight, and successor state then form the LBO transition.

The set 𝒮\mathcal{S} prevents repeated hidden batches for a given successor and excludes the current real batch during online LBO. The list 𝒞\mathcal{C} contains the accepted hidden batches. Initial and online transition limits LL and the generation schedule are specified in Table C3.

Successor selection and TD target. For a replay transition ξi=(si,Ai,Ri,wi,si′)\xi_{i}=(s_{i},A_{i},R_{i},w_{i},s^{\prime}_{i}), the TD target combines its observed reward with an estimate of weighted future discoveries. To estimate this successor value, the current acquisition function scores every candidate in the recorded successor pool Ui′U^{\prime}_{i} using

qθ​(si′,x)=p^i′​(x)+fθ​(si′,ci′​(x)),x∈Ui′.q_{\theta}(s^{\prime}_{i},x)=\hat{p}^{\prime}_{i}(x)+f_{\theta}(s^{\prime}_{i},c^{\prime}_{i}(x)),\qquad x\in U^{\prime}_{i}. (21)

The state si′s^{\prime}_{i}, candidate features ci′​(x)c^{\prime}_{i}(x), and hit probabilities p^i′​(x)\hat{p}^{\prime}_{i}(x) are saved when the transition is constructed. Replay keeps these inputs fixed and applies the current network to them. As θ\theta changes, the network can select a different successor batch from the same recorded pool.

Following Double DQN, we select the BB candidates with the highest current scores to form Aθ,i′A^{\prime}_{\theta,i} and evaluate them with the target network (van Hasselt et al., 2016). This gives

Qθ¯​(si′,Aθ,i′)\displaystyle Q_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime}_{i},A^{\prime}_{\theta,i}) =∑x∈Aθ,i′[p^i′​(x)+fθ¯​(si′,ci′​(x))],\displaystyle=\sum\nolimits_{x\in A^{\prime}_{\theta,i}}\left[\hat{p}^{\prime}_{i}(x)+f_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime}_{i},c^{\prime}_{i}(x))\right], (22)
Yi\displaystyle Y_{i} =Ri+wi​Qθ¯​(si′,Aθ,i′).\displaystyle=R_{i}+w_{i}Q_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime}_{i},A^{\prime}_{\theta,i}).

This successor selection is used to calculate the training target and does not trigger additional experiments. For terminal transitions, Yi=RiY_{i}=R_{i}. Real and LBO transitions use the same target, which is held constant when computing gradients.

Experience replay and parameter updates. Real and LBO transitions enter a shared prioritized replay buffer. Let nn be the number of stored transitions and ρi\rho_{i} the priority of transition ii. Each update samples a training batch ℬ\mathcal{B} without replacement using normalized sampling weights

P⁡(i)=(ρi+ϵPER)αPER∑j=1n(ρj+ϵPER)αPER.P(i)=\frac{(\rho_{i}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{PER}})^{\alpha_{\mathrm{PER}}}}{\sum\nolimits_{j=1}^{n}(\rho_{j}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{PER}})^{\alpha_{\mathrm{PER}}}}. (23)

The exponent αPER\alpha_{\mathrm{PER}} controls the preference for high priority transitions. Frequently sampled transitions receive smaller importance weights in the loss, reducing the imbalance introduced by prioritized sampling. We use

κ~i=(n​P​(i))−βIS,κiIS=κ~imaxj∈ℬ⁡κ~j.\widetilde{\kappa}_{i}=(nP(i))^{-\beta_{\mathrm{IS}}},\qquad\kappa_{i}^{\mathrm{IS}}=\frac{\widetilde{\kappa}_{i}}{\max\nolimits_{j\in\mathcal{B}}\widetilde{\kappa}_{j}}. (24)

Here, βIS\beta_{\mathrm{IS}} controls the strength of the weighting, and normalization sets the largest weight within ℬ\mathcal{B} to one. With TD error δi=Qθ​(si,Ai)−Yi\delta_{i}=Q_{\theta}(s_{i},A_{i})-Y_{i}, the training loss is

ℒ^TD​(θ)=1|ℬ|​∑i∈ℬκiIS​Huber1⁡(δi).\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{TD}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum\nolimits_{i\in\mathcal{B}}\kappa_{i}^{\mathrm{IS}}\operatorname{Huber}_{1}(\delta_{i}). (25)

The Huber loss is quadratic for absolute errors up to 1 and linear above 1. Gradients update only θ\theta, with surrogate predictions held fixed. After each update, the sampled transitions receive priorities ρi←|δi|+ϵPER\rho_{i}\leftarrow|\delta_{i}|+\epsilon_{\mathrm{PER}}, and the target parameters follow

θ¯←(1−τtarget)​θ¯+τtarget​θ.\bar{\theta}\leftarrow(1-\tau_{\mathrm{target}})\bar{\theta}+\tau_{\mathrm{target}}\theta. (26)

The optimizer and training settings are specified in Table C3.

Appendix B Theoretical Analysis

We prove Propositions 1–3, establishing weighted Bellman optimality, relating the Hellinger weight to predictive improvement, and bounding the gap in final discoveries.

B.1  Weighted Bellman Optimality

We fix the surrogate training and prediction procedures and condition on their randomness. Given the history HtH_{t} and query batch AtA_{t}, the observed outcomes determine the discovery count RtR_{t} and feedback weight wt=w⁡(Ht,At,Ht+1)∈[0,1]w_{t}=w(H_{t},A_{t},H_{t+1})\in[0,1]. Both quantities are therefore determined by the successor history Ht+1H_{t+1}. At history HH, the feasible batch set is

𝒜t​(H)={A⊆Ut​(H):|A|=B}.\mathcal{A}_{t}(H)=\{A\subseteq U_{t}(H):|A|=B\}. (27)

For any selection policy π\pi, define the weighted discovery count from round tt to the end of screening as

Gtw=∑k=tT−1(∏j=tk−1wj)​Rk,GTw=0.G_{t}^{w}=\sum\nolimits_{k=t}^{T-1}\left(\prod\nolimits_{j=t}^{k-1}w_{j}\right)R_{k},\qquad G_{T}^{w}=0. (28)

The current count RtR_{t} has weight one, while each subsequent count is weighted by the product of the intervening feedback weights. The corresponding policy value is

Vtw,π​(H)=𝔼π​[Gtw∣Ht=H],V_{t}^{w,\pi}(H)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[G_{t}^{w}\mid H_{t}=H], (29)

the expected weighted number of remaining discoveries when selection follows π\pi from the current screening history HH. The terminal value is zero because no experiments remain.

Separating the current round from subsequent rounds gives

Gtw=Rt+wt​Gt+1w.G_{t}^{w}=R_{t}+w_{t}G_{t+1}^{w}. (30)

Given Ht+1H_{t+1}, both RtR_{t} and wtw_{t} are known, and the conditional expectation of the remaining return is Vt+1w,π​(Ht+1)V_{t+1}^{w,\pi}(H_{t+1}). Averaging over the current batch and its observations, we obtain the following by the law of iterated expectations:

Vtw,π(H)=∑A∈𝒜t​(H)πt(A∣H)𝔼[Rt+wtVt+1w,π(Ht+1)∣Ht=H,At=A].V_{t}^{w,\pi}(H)=\sum\nolimits_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{t}(H)}\pi_{t}(A\mid H)\mathbb{E}\!\left[R_{t}+w_{t}V_{t+1}^{w,\pi}(H_{t+1})\mid H_{t}=H,A_{t}=A\right]. (31)

Here, πt​(A∣H)\pi_{t}(A\mid H) is the probability of selecting batch AA given history HH. This expression averages the expected current discoveries and weighted successor value over the policy’s batch choices.

Starting from the terminal condition VT∗,w=0V_{T}^{*,w}=0, define recursively

Qt∗,w​(H,A)\displaystyle Q_{t}^{*,w}(H,A) =𝔼[Rt+wtVt+1∗,w(Ht+1)∣Ht=H,At=A],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[R_{t}+w_{t}V_{t+1}^{*,w}(H_{t+1})\mid H_{t}=H,A_{t}=A\right], (32)
Vt∗,w​(H)\displaystyle V_{t}^{*,w}(H) =maxA∈𝒜t​(H)⁡Qt∗,w​(H,A).\displaystyle=\max\nolimits_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{t}(H)}Q_{t}^{*,w}(H,A).

This recursion starts at the last round, where only current discoveries contribute. Earlier rounds also include the weighted successor value already determined at the next round. Here, Qt∗,w​(H,A)Q_{t}^{*,w}(H,A) is the conditional expected value of selecting batch AA, and Vt∗,w​(H)V_{t}^{*,w}(H) takes the maximum over feasible batches. The finite horizon and finite batch sets uniquely determine these values. Since 0≤Rt≤B0\leq R_{t}\leq B and 0≤wt≤10\leq w_{t}\leq 1,

0≤Qt∗,w​(H,A)≤Vt∗,w​(H)≤(T−t)​B.0\leq Q_{t}^{*,w}(H,A)\leq V_{t}^{*,w}(H)\leq(T-t)B. (33)

To establish optimality, we first show that every policy has value at most Vt∗,wV_{t}^{*,w}. At the terminal round t=Tt=T, every policy satisfies

VTw,π​(H)=VT∗,w​(H)=0.V_{T}^{w,\pi}(H)=V_{T}^{*,w}(H)=0. (34)

Suppose that, at round t+1t+1, every policy and reachable history satisfy

Vt+1w,π​(Ht+1)≤Vt+1∗,w​(Ht+1).V_{t+1}^{w,\pi}(H_{t+1})\leq V_{t+1}^{*,w}(H_{t+1}). (35)

At round tt, retain the policy’s current batch selection probabilities and replace its successor value by this upper bound. Since wt≥0w_{t}\geq 0, this replacement cannot decrease the conditional expected value. Equations 31 and 32 therefore give

Vtw,π​(H)\displaystyle V_{t}^{w,\pi}(H) ≤∑A∈𝒜t​(H)πt(A∣H)𝔼[Rt+wtVt+1∗,w(Ht+1)∣Ht=H,At=A]\displaystyle\leq\sum\nolimits_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{t}(H)}\pi_{t}(A\mid H)\mathbb{E}\!\left[R_{t}+w_{t}V_{t+1}^{*,w}(H_{t+1})\mid H_{t}=H,A_{t}=A\right] (36)
=∑A∈𝒜t​(H)πt​(A∣H)​Qt∗,w​(H,A)\displaystyle=\sum\nolimits_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{t}(H)}\pi_{t}(A\mid H)Q_{t}^{*,w}(H,A)
≤Vt∗,w​(H).\displaystyle\leq V_{t}^{*,w}(H).

The last inequality holds because any probability-weighted average of batch values cannot exceed their maximum. Thus, the value bound at the next round implies the bound at the current round. Backward induction from the terminal round establishes Vtw,π​(H)≤Vt∗,w​(H)V_{t}^{w,\pi}(H)\leq V_{t}^{*,w}(H) for every round, policy, and reachable history.

We next show that this upper bound is attained. Let πw∗\pi_{w}^{*} select a feasible batch maximizing Qt∗,wQ_{t}^{*,w} at every round and reachable history. At the terminal round,

VTw,πw∗​(H)=VT∗,w​(H)=0.V_{T}^{w,\pi_{w}^{*}}(H)=V_{T}^{*,w}(H)=0. (37)

Suppose this policy attains Vt+1∗,wV_{t+1}^{*,w} at every reachable history at round t+1t+1. After selecting πw∗​(H)\pi_{w}^{*}(H) at round tt, its continuation therefore attains the optimal successor value in the definition of Qt∗,wQ_{t}^{*,w}.

Vtw,πw∗​(H)\displaystyle V_{t}^{w,\pi_{w}^{*}}(H) =Qt∗,w​(H,πw∗​(H))\displaystyle=Q_{t}^{*,w}\bigl(H,\pi_{w}^{*}(H)\bigr) (38)
=maxA∈𝒜t​(H)⁡Qt∗,w​(H,A)\displaystyle=\max\nolimits_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{t}(H)}Q_{t}^{*,w}(H,A)
=Vt∗,w​(H).\displaystyle=V_{t}^{*,w}(H).

The first equality follows from the induction hypothesis, the second from the policy’s maximizing batch choice, and the third from the definition of Vt∗,wV_{t}^{*,w}. Backward induction therefore establishes that this policy attains the bound at every round and reachable history.

Finally, since Jw​(π)=V0w,π​(H0)J_{w}(\pi)=V_{0}^{w,\pi}(H_{0}), every policy’s objective is bounded above by V0∗,w​(H0)V_{0}^{*,w}(H_{0}), and πw∗\pi_{w}^{*} attains this value. Therefore,

Jw​(πw∗)\displaystyle J_{w}(\pi_{w}^{*}) =V0w,πw∗​(H0)=V0∗,w​(H0)\displaystyle=V_{0}^{w,\pi_{w}^{*}}(H_{0})=V_{0}^{*,w}(H_{0}) (39)
=maxA∈𝒜0​(H0)⁡Q0∗,w​(H0,A)=maxπ⁡Jw​(π).\displaystyle=\max\nolimits_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{0}(H_{0})}Q_{0}^{*,w}(H_{0},A)=\max\nolimits_{\pi}J_{w}(\pi).

Thus, maximizing the optimal batch value at each round maximizes the weighted cumulative discovery objective. This proves Proposition 1.

B.2  Feedback and Predictive Improvement

Fix the current history HtH_{t} and query batch AtA_{t}, with remaining pool U=Ut+1U=U_{t+1} and |U|>0|U|>0. Under a common joint probability model, define the conditional hit probabilities before and after feedback as

px\displaystyle p_{x} =Pr⁡(z⁡(x)=1∣Ht,At),\displaystyle=\Pr(z(x)=1\mid H_{t},A_{t}), (40)
qx\displaystyle q_{x} =Pr⁡(z⁡(x)=1∣Ht,At,Ot).\displaystyle=\Pr(z(x)=1\mid H_{t},A_{t},O_{t}).

We analyze the Hellinger weight computed from these probabilities. Before the batch outcomes are observed, averaging the updated probability qxq_{x} over their possible values recovers the current probability pxp_{x}, giving

𝔼[qx∣Ht,At]=px.\mathbb{E}[q_{x}\mid H_{t},A_{t}]=p_{x}. (41)

This analysis uses conditional hit probabilities before and after experimental feedback. TDAL approximates these probabilities using MC dropout predictions.

The expected reduction in mean squared prediction error is

Δpred=1|U|​∑x∈U𝔼⁡[(px−z⁡(x))2−(qx−z⁡(x))2].\Delta_{\mathrm{pred}}=\frac{1}{|U|}\sum\nolimits_{x\in U}\mathbb{E}\!\left[(p_{x}-z(x))^{2}-(q_{x}-z(x))^{2}\right]. (42)

The two terms are the binary Brier losses before and after feedback (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). Expanding their difference gives

(px−z⁡(x))2−(qx−z⁡(x))2=(qx−px)2+2​(qx−px)​(z⁡(x)−qx).(p_{x}-z(x))^{2}-(q_{x}-z(x))^{2}=(q_{x}-p_{x})^{2}+2(q_{x}-p_{x})(z(x)-q_{x}). (43)

By the definition of qxq_{x},

𝔼[z(x)−qx∣Ht,At,Ot]=Pr(z(x)=1∣Ht,At,Ot)−qx=0.\mathbb{E}[z(x)-q_{x}\mid H_{t},A_{t},O_{t}]=\Pr(z(x)=1\mid H_{t},A_{t},O_{t})-q_{x}=0. (44)

Given the feedback, qx−pxq_{x}-p_{x} is fixed, so the cross term has zero conditional expectation. The law of iterated expectations therefore yields

Δpred=1|U|​∑x∈U𝔼⁡[(qx−px)2].\Delta_{\mathrm{pred}}=\frac{1}{|U|}\sum\nolimits_{x\in U}\mathbb{E}[(q_{x}-p_{x})^{2}]. (45)

Thus, feedback does not increase mean prediction error in expectation, and the expected reduction equals the mean squared change in hit probabilities.

To relate this reduction to the Hellinger weight, write

hx2\displaystyle h_{x}^{2} =1−px​qx−(1−px)​(1−qx),\displaystyle=1-\sqrt{p_{x}q_{x}}-\sqrt{(1-p_{x})(1-q_{x})}, (46)
wt2\displaystyle w_{t}^{2} =1|U|​∑x∈Uhx2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|U|}\sum\nolimits_{x\in U}h_{x}^{2}.

For any p,q∈[0,1]p,q\in[0,1], let h=HBer​(p,q)h=H_{\mathrm{Ber}}(p,q). The Bernoulli Hellinger bounds (Sason and Verdú, 2016) follow directly here. Since a​b≥min⁡(a,b)\sqrt{ab}\geq\min(a,b),

h2≤1−min⁡(p,q)−min⁡(1−p,1−q)=|p−q|.h^{2}\leq 1-\min(p,q)-\min(1-p,1-q)=|p-q|. (47)

Conversely, define

u=(p,1−p),v=(q,1−q).u=(\sqrt{p},\sqrt{1-p}),\qquad v=(\sqrt{q},\sqrt{1-q}). (48)

Cauchy–Schwarz gives

|p−q|\displaystyle|p-q| =12​∑i=12|ui−vi|​|ui+vi|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{2}|u_{i}-v_{i}|\,|u_{i}+v_{i}| (49)
≤12​‖u−v‖2​‖u+v‖2=h​2−h2≤2​h.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\|u-v\|_{2}\|u+v\|_{2}=h\sqrt{2-h^{2}}\leq\sqrt{2}\,h.

Hence

hx4≤(qx−px)2≤2​hx2.h_{x}^{4}\leq(q_{x}-p_{x})^{2}\leq 2h_{x}^{2}. (50)

Jensen’s inequality gives, for each feedback outcome,

wt4\displaystyle w_{t}^{4} =(1|U|​∑x∈Uhx2)2\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{|U|}\sum\nolimits_{x\in U}h_{x}^{2}\right)^{2} (51)
≤1|U|​∑x∈Uhx4\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{|U|}\sum\nolimits_{x\in U}h_{x}^{4}
≤1|U|​∑x∈U(qx−px)2≤2​wt2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{|U|}\sum\nolimits_{x\in U}(q_{x}-p_{x})^{2}\leq 2w_{t}^{2}.

Taking conditional expectations gives

𝔼⁡[wt4]≤Δpred≤2​𝔼​[wt2].\mathbb{E}[w_{t}^{4}]\leq\Delta_{\mathrm{pred}}\leq 2\mathbb{E}[w_{t}^{2}]. (52)

An experiment therefore does more than establish whether queried candidates are hits. It can improve predictions for unmeasured candidates. These bounds connect that expected improvement to the Hellinger weight, supporting the use of feedback’s effect on remaining predictions to weight successor value.

Now consider querying one candidate aa and observing only its hit indicator. Suppress conditioning on the current history and query, and define

r\displaystyle r =Pr⁡(z⁡(a)=1)∈(0,1),\displaystyle=\Pr(z(a)=1)\in(0,1), (53)
px+\displaystyle p_{x}^{+} =Pr⁡(z⁡(x)=1∣z⁡(a)=1),\displaystyle=\Pr(z(x)=1\mid z(a)=1),
px−\displaystyle p_{x}^{-} =Pr⁡(z⁡(x)=1∣z⁡(a)=0).\displaystyle=\Pr(z(x)=1\mid z(a)=0).

The law of total probability gives

px=r​px++(1−r)​px−.p_{x}=rp_{x}^{+}+(1-r)p_{x}^{-}. (54)

After feedback, qx=px+q_{x}=p_{x}^{+} with probability rr and qx=px−q_{x}=p_{x}^{-} with probability 1−r1-r. Hence

𝔼⁡[(qx−px)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(q_{x}-p_{x})^{2}] =r​(px+−px)2+(1−r)​(px−−px)2\displaystyle=r(p_{x}^{+}-p_{x})^{2}+(1-r)(p_{x}^{-}-p_{x})^{2} (55)
=r​(1−r)2​(px+−px−)2+(1−r)​r2​(px+−px−)2\displaystyle=r(1-r)^{2}(p_{x}^{+}-p_{x}^{-})^{2}+(1-r)r^{2}(p_{x}^{+}-p_{x}^{-})^{2}
=r⁡(1−r)​(px+−px−)2.\displaystyle=r(1-r)(p_{x}^{+}-p_{x}^{-})^{2}.

Averaging over the remaining candidates yields

Δpred​(a)=r⁡(1−r)|U|​∑x∈U(px+−px−)2.\Delta_{\mathrm{pred}}(a)=\frac{r(1-r)}{|U|}\sum\nolimits_{x\in U}(p_{x}^{+}-p_{x}^{-})^{2}. (56)

This proves Proposition 2.

Outcome uncertainty and its influence on remaining candidates jointly determine predictive improvement. If neither outcome changes remaining predictions, the feedback provides no predictive improvement. Otherwise, even a query without a hit changes remaining predictions and produces a nonzero weight. This explains how TDAL retains the current discovery reward while allowing experiments without hits to contribute to learning through successor value.

The decomposition into two outcomes is the special case of one query revealing only a binary label. TDAL observes a batch of continuous phenotypes instead. The general identity for predictive improvement conditions on the complete batch observations OtO_{t} and also applies to that feedback under the same assumptions about the joint model. It does not require a binary observation space.

B.3  Final Discovery Gap

Fix the initial history H0H_{0}, surrogate update rule, and algorithmic randomness. At each round, 0≤Rt≤B0\leq R_{t}\leq B, and the feedback weight is a measurable function wt=w⁡(Ht,At,Ht+1)∈[0,1]w_{t}=w(H_{t},A_{t},H_{t+1})\in[0,1]. This permits the weight, current discovery count, and successor value to depend on the same feedback. Write

Wt=∏j=0t−1wj,W0=1.W_{t}=\prod\nolimits_{j=0}^{t-1}w_{j},\qquad W_{0}=1. (57)

At each history HH, let s=st​(H)s=s_{t}(H) be the screening state and let θ\theta denote the network parameters after all online updates at that history. The learned policy selects a feasible batch maximizing Qθ​(s,A)Q_{\theta}(s,A). Its value estimation error is

εtw​(H)=maxA∈𝒜t​(H)⁡|Qθ​(s,A)−Qt∗,w​(H,A)|.\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H)=\max\nolimits_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{t}(H)}|Q_{\theta}(s,A)-Q_{t}^{*,w}(H,A)|. (58)

First consider how this error affects the current batch choice. Fix a history HH, let A∗A^{*} maximize Qt∗,w​(H,A)Q_{t}^{*,w}(H,A), and let A^\widehat{A} maximize Qθ​(s,A)Q_{\theta}(s,A). By the error definition,

Vt∗,w​(H)\displaystyle V_{t}^{*,w}(H) =Qt∗,w​(H,A∗)\displaystyle=Q_{t}^{*,w}(H,A^{*}) (59)
≤Qθ​(s,A∗)+εtw​(H)\displaystyle\leq Q_{\theta}(s,A^{*})+\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H)
≤Qθ​(s,A^)+εtw​(H)\displaystyle\leq Q_{\theta}(s,\widehat{A})+\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H)
≤Qt∗,w​(H,A^)+2​εtw​(H).\displaystyle\leq Q_{t}^{*,w}(H,\widehat{A})+2\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H).

The second inequality uses the maximizing property of A^\widehat{A}. Thus,

0≤Vt∗,w​(H)−Qt∗,w​(H,A^)≤2​εtw​(H).0\leq V_{t}^{*,w}(H)-Q_{t}^{*,w}(H,\widehat{A})\leq 2\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H). (60)

The gap between the optimal batch value and the value of the selected batch is therefore at most twice the estimation error.

Next, accumulate these losses across the screening trajectory. Let A^t\widehat{A}_{t} be the batch selected by the learned policy at round tt. The weighted Bellman equation gives

Qt∗,w(Ht,A^t)=𝔼[Rt+wtVt+1∗,w(Ht+1)∣Ht,At=A^t].Q_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t},\widehat{A}_{t})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[R_{t}+w_{t}V_{t+1}^{*,w}(H_{t+1})\mid H_{t},A_{t}=\widehat{A}_{t}\right]. (61)

Since WtW_{t} is determined by the current history and Wt+1=Wt​wtW_{t+1}=W_{t}w_{t}, taking expectations along the learned policy gives

𝔼πθ​[∑t=0T−1Wt​(Vt∗,w​(Ht)−Qt∗,w​(Ht,A^t))∣H0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}W_{t}\bigl(V_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t})-Q_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t},\widehat{A}_{t})\bigr)\mid H_{0}\right] (62)
=𝔼πθ​[∑t=0T−1(Wt​Vt∗,w​(Ht)−Wt​Rt−Wt+1​Vt+1∗,w​(Ht+1))∣H0]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}\bigl(W_{t}V_{t}^{*,w}(H_{t})-W_{t}R_{t}-W_{t+1}V_{t+1}^{*,w}(H_{t+1})\bigr)\mid H_{0}\right]
=V0∗,w​(H0)−Jw​(πθ).\displaystyle=V_{0}^{*,w}(H_{0})-J_{w}(\pi_{\theta}).

Value terms from adjacent rounds cancel, leaving the initial value V0∗,w​(H0)V_{0}^{*,w}(H_{0}). The terminal term vanishes because VT∗,w=0V_{T}^{*,w}=0. Proposition 1 and the batch value gap then imply

maxπ⁡Jw​(π)−Jw​(πθ)≤2​𝔼πθ​[∑t=0T−1Wt​εtw​(Ht)∣H0].\max\nolimits_{\pi}J_{w}(\pi)-J_{w}(\pi_{\theta})\leq 2\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}W_{t}\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H_{t})\mid H_{0}\right]. (63)

Finally, relate the weighted objective to final discoveries. Since

CT=C0+∑t=0T−1Rt,C_{T}=C_{0}+\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}R_{t}, (64)

every policy satisfies

𝔼π​[CT∣H0]=C0+Jw​(π)+𝔼π​[∑t=0T−1(1−Wt)​Rt∣H0].\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[C_{T}\mid H_{0}]=C_{0}+J_{w}(\pi)+\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}(1-W_{t})R_{t}\mid H_{0}\right]. (65)

The last term counts the expected discoveries omitted when each round receives weight WtW_{t} instead of one. It is nonnegative because Rt≥0R_{t}\geq 0 and Wt≤1W_{t}\leq 1. Let πC∗\pi_{C}^{*} maximize expected final discoveries under the same initial information and budget, and write

ΔC​(w)=𝔼πC∗​[∑t=0T−1(1−Wt)​Rt∣H0].\Delta_{C}(w)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{C}^{*}}\!\left[\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}(1-W_{t})R_{t}\mid H_{0}\right]. (66)

Subtracting the final discovery counts and using the nonnegative weighting bias of the learned policy gives

𝔼πC∗​[CT∣H0]−𝔼πθ​[CT∣H0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{C}^{*}}[C_{T}\mid H_{0}]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[C_{T}\mid H_{0}] (67)
≤ΔC​(w)+Jw​(πC∗)−Jw​(πθ)\displaystyle\leq\Delta_{C}(w)+J_{w}(\pi_{C}^{*})-J_{w}(\pi_{\theta})
≤ΔC​(w)+maxπ⁡Jw​(π)−Jw​(πθ)\displaystyle\leq\Delta_{C}(w)+\max\nolimits_{\pi}J_{w}(\pi)-J_{w}(\pi_{\theta})
≤ΔC​(w)+2​𝔼πθ​[∑t=0T−1Wt​εtw​(Ht)∣H0].\displaystyle\leq\Delta_{C}(w)+2\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}W_{t}\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H_{t})\mid H_{0}\right].

This proves Proposition 3.

Feedback weights and the two error terms. Consider two weight rules w,w′w,w^{\prime} in the same experimental environment. If, at every reachable history, batch, and feedback outcome,

w′​(H,A,H′)≥w⁡(H,A,H′),w^{\prime}(H,A,H^{\prime})\geq w(H,A,H^{\prime}), (68)

then Wt′≥WtW_{t}^{\prime}\geq W_{t} on every trajectory. Taking expectations under the same optimal discovery policy πC∗\pi_{C}^{*} yields

ΔC​(w′)≤ΔC​(w).\Delta_{C}(w^{\prime})\leq\Delta_{C}(w). (69)

Thus, increasing feedback weights reduces the objective weighting bias.

To examine the error term, consider constant weights wt=ww_{t}=w and assume all weight settings being compared share a common value error bound

εtw​(H)≤ε.\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H)\leq\varepsilon. (70)

Then Wt=wtW_{t}=w^{t}, and Rt≤BR_{t}\leq B gives

ΔC​(w)≤B​∑t=0T−1(1−wt),\Delta_{C}(w)\leq B\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}(1-w^{t}), (71)

while

2​𝔼πθ​[∑t=0T−1Wt​εtw​(Ht)∣H0]≤2​ε​∑t=0T−1wt.2\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}W_{t}\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H_{t})\mid H_{0}\right]\leq 2\varepsilon\sum\nolimits_{t=0}^{T-1}w^{t}. (72)

The bias bound is nonincreasing in ww, whereas the estimation error term’s bound is nondecreasing under the common error bound ε\varepsilon. Smaller weights reduce the error bound but attenuate more future discovery return. Larger weights retain more future return but increase the error bound. In the learned model, εtw​(H)\varepsilon_{t}^{w}(H) and the selected trajectory depend on ww. Comparing weight settings therefore also involves their different value estimation errors. When w=1w=1, the objective weighting bias vanishes and the final discovery gap is at most 2​T​ε2T\varepsilon. If also ε=0\varepsilon=0, the learned policy achieves the optimal expected final discovery count.

Appendix C Datasets and Experimental Setup

C.1  Datasets and Hit Definitions

The eight public screens comprise four single gene tasks, three double gene tasks, and one triple gene task, covering T cell function, cancer cell growth, immune killing, and genetic interactions. Each candidate is a single gene or combinatorial perturbation. Table C1 summarizes perturbation types, phenotypes, and hit rules.

Raw phenotype scores are transformed into effects e⁡(x)e(x) according to the direction in the table. For a pool of N=|𝒳|N=|\mathcal{X}| candidates, the score at rank max⁡{1,⌊0.05​N⌋}\max\{1,\lfloor 0.05N\rfloor\} in descending effect order defines the fixed threshold τ\tau, with hits given by z(x)=𝟏{e(x)≥τ}z(x)=\mathbf{1}\{e(x)\geq\tau\}. The target hit proportion is 5%, and τ\tau is the corresponding phenotype score threshold. The threshold is fixed before screening. The phenotype and hit label of each candidate are revealed when it is queried.

IFN-γ\gamma. This task identifies genes that regulate interferon-γ\gamma production in T cells. Enrichment differences between populations with high and low cytokine levels measure perturbation effects. We target strong effects in either direction (Schmidt et al., 2022).

IL-2. This task identifies regulators of interleukin-2 production following T cell stimulation. Enrichment differences between populations with high and low expression define the phenotype, with strong effects in either direction included as discovery targets (Schmidt et al., 2022).

NK. This task studies cancer cell genes that affect sensitivity or resistance to natural killer cells. The phenotype is the sum of standardized enrichment scores across two replicates for perturbed K562 cells exposed to NK cells relative to controls. Strong effects in either direction are targeted (Zhuang et al., 2019).

Carnevale. This task studies genes that affect T cell proliferation under immunosuppressive conditions. We use enrichment scores associated with proliferation from the screen under adenosine suppression and target perturbations that strongly increase or decrease proliferation (Carnevale et al., 2022).

Simpson K562. The original study examines how DNA repair genes jointly affect cell growth and PARP inhibitor response. We use its double gene CRISPRi growth phenotype and target combinations with the highest growth scores (Simpson et al., 2023).

SCHEMATIC. This task seeks gene combinations that cause synthetic lethality across cancer cell backgrounds. We use the multilineage interaction score to identify strong negative interactions whose growth or survival defects exceed expectations from individual perturbations (Fong et al., 2025).

Kuzmin yeast. This task examines how duplicate genes compensate for one another and how this compensation depends on other genes. We use the corrected trigenic interaction score to target combinations with stronger growth defects than expected (Kuzmin et al., 2020).

Horlbeck Jurkat. This task examines the effect of jointly repressing two genes on Jurkat cell growth. We use the double gene CRISPRi growth phenotype and target combinations that strongly inhibit growth (Horlbeck et al., 2018).

C.2  Experimental Protocol and Hyperparameters

Table C2 summarizes candidate counts, pool hit counts, and screening configurations.

NN is the number of queryable perturbations with valid measured phenotypes and fixed representations in the retrospective evaluation. Combinatorial tasks count gene combinations as candidates. All candidate identities and representations are known at the start. Each method initially receives the phenotypes of the n0n_{0} candidates in D0D_{0}, while the phenotypes of the remaining N−n0N-n_{0} candidates are withheld. After batch AtA_{t} is selected, the evaluation environment returns its recorded experimental outcomes, adds these observations to the measured data, and removes the candidates from the unmeasured pool. Screening returns all verified hit candidates, whose count CTC_{T} measures final discovery.

For seed ii, let Ct,iC_{t,i} be the number of hits in the measured set after tt active rounds, with C0,iC_{0,i} the number in the initial set. The final cumulative hit count is

CT,i=C0,i+∑t=0T−1Rt,i.C_{T,i}=C_{0,i}+\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}R_{t,i}. (73)

This metric counts distinct discovered hits within the total budget, including initialization. Recall is CT,iC_{T,i} divided by the fixed pool hit count in Table C2. Batch size BB gives the number of new queries per round, TT is the number of active rounds, and the total budget M=n0+B​TM=n_{0}+BT includes initialization and all subsequent queries.

Each task is repeated with seeds 0–4. Methods share the candidate pool, initial set, hit threshold, experimental budget, and underlying phenotype dataset within each seed. Method differences are paired within each task and seed before aggregation across seeds.

Hyperparameter settings. Table C3 summarizes TDAL’s model and training settings.

C.3  Baseline Methods

For batch perturbation screening, we compare representative methods for hit discovery, Bayesian optimization, and batch active learning, with random selection as a reference. UCB, EI, TS, TopUncertain, and OAE use the GeneDisco Bayesian MLP and retrain their surrogate after each round of new observations (Mehrjou et al., 2022).

PoH. Many Needles selects the BB unmeasured candidates with the highest estimated probability of exceeding the hit threshold (Rubbi et al., 2026). At each round, we refit a Bayesian MLP with two hidden layers of widths 128 and 64 on the measured data. For each candidate x∈Utx\in U_{t}, we obtain 50 MC dropout predictions and use their mean and standard deviation to form a Gaussian predictive approximation. The probability of exceeding τ\tau then serves as the acquisition score.

OAE. OAE uses optimistic estimates for batch discovery of candidates with high responses. We use its released Bayesian variant, which combines predictive means and uncertainty to select each batch after aligning predictions with the effect direction (Pacchiano et al., 2023).

DiscoBAX. DiscoBAX targets a diverse subset of candidates with high responses and uses fantasized observations to estimate information gain about that subset. We use the authors’ surrogate training and acquisition implementation, with two hidden layers of 128 and 64 units and dropout 0.2 to match TDAL and PoH in network capacity. We evaluate this implementation on the four single gene perturbation tasks (Lyle et al., 2023).

UCB. Upper Confidence Bound combines the predictive mean with a weighted uncertainty term. It favors candidates with high predicted effects or high uncertainty to balance exploitation and exploration (Srinivas et al., 2010).

Expected Improvement (EI). EI estimates the expected improvement over the best effect observed so far and prioritizes candidates with larger expected gains (Jones et al., 1998).

Thompson Sampling (TS). TS draws an effect function from the surrogate posterior and selects a batch by ranking unmeasured candidates under that draw, allowing model uncertainty to influence selection (Thompson, 1933).

TopUncertain. TopUncertain ranks candidates by predictive standard deviation and allocates experiments to regions where the surrogate is most uncertain (Mehrjou et al., 2022).

BADGE. BADGE selects diverse batches using k-means++ in a gradient representation space. We use the GeneDisco regression implementation and its proxy gradient representations (Ash et al., 2020; Mehrjou et al., 2022).

CoreSet. CoreSet greedily expands geometric coverage in the candidate representation space extracted by the surrogate. It successively selects the candidate farthest from the existing selection centers (Sener and Savarese, 2018).

KMeans-Embedding. This method uses k-means to cluster candidate representations extracted by the surrogate and selects candidates near cluster centers to represent different regions of the candidate space (Mehrjou et al., 2022).

Random. Random samples uniformly without replacement from the current unmeasured pool, providing a reference for random screening.

Omitting each task in turn leaves TDAL with the best average rank over the remaining seven tasks. Thus, its leading average rank does not depend on any single task.

Appendix E Landscape Structure and Active Discovery

E.1  Local Hit Enrichment and Discovery Gains on Real Tasks

Local hit enrichment. We compare the hit fraction around hit candidates with the overall hit fraction in the analysis sample to measure how hits cluster in candidate representation space. Neighbors are determined by cosine distance after standardizing the fixed candidate representations ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) and applying L2 normalization.

For each task, we randomly sample hit candidates and other candidates in their proportions in the full candidate pool, forming an analysis sample 𝒫\mathcal{P} of at most 10,000 candidates. Let 𝒫+={x∈𝒫:z⁡(x)=1}\mathcal{P}_{+}=\{x\in\mathcal{P}:z(x)=1\} be its hit set. For each hit candidate xx, let 𝒩10​(x)\mathcal{N}_{10}(x) contain the ten nearest other candidates within 𝒫\mathcal{P}. We compute the hit fraction among these ten neighbors, average it over all hit candidates, and divide by the overall hit fraction in the sample to obtain

Enrich10=1|𝒫+|​∑x∈𝒫+110​∑y∈𝒩10​(x)z⁡(y)|𝒫+|/|𝒫|.\operatorname{Enrich}_{10}=\frac{\displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{+}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}_{+}}\frac{1}{10}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{N}_{10}(x)}z(y)}{\displaystyle|\mathcal{P}_{+}|/|\mathcal{P}|}. (74)

The numerator is the mean neighbor hit fraction around hit candidates, and the denominator is the overall hit fraction in the analysis sample. For example, an overall hit fraction of 5% and a mean neighbor hit fraction of 15% give 3×3\times enrichment. Values above one indicate that other hits are more common near hit candidates. Values near one indicate a similar hit fraction to the sample overall, and values below one indicate a lower local hit fraction. We repeat sampling and calculation three times for each task. Table E1 reports the mean enrichment over these three samples.

Discovery gains. For each task, we divide each method’s final cumulative hit count by Random’s count under the same seed, then average over five seeds. The shared methods are PoH, OAE, UCB, EI, TS, TopUncertain, BADGE, CoreSet, and KMeans-Embedding. Their average gain is the mean of these nine methods’ results. Across the eight tasks, this average gain increases with local hit enrichment (Spearman ρ=0.95\rho=0.95, n=8n=8). Both enrichment and discovery gains are near random levels on NK and higher on Simpson K562, showing a close association between local hit structure and active discovery gains across tasks.

E.2  Noisy Multicluster Landscapes

Landscape construction. We construct landscapes in which hits are dispersed or concentrated in six clusters. The 17,660 candidates have fixed two-dimensional coordinates that are defined without phenotype information. KMeans divides these coordinates into six regions, each with a response peak at its center.

Within each region, candidates closer to the center receive higher response scores. We sort candidates by distance, negate their ranks, and divide by the region’s hit quota. The quotas are 148 for one region and 147 for each of the other five, giving 883 hits in total. This scaling produces clusters of similar hit counts when no noise is added. We standardize the scores across candidates and mix them with independent standardized Gaussian noise. Increasing the noise contribution disperses hits away from the cluster centers.

To keep phenotype values comparable, we rank the mixed scores and assign them the same fixed set of standard normal quantiles. The top 5% are designated as hits. All settings therefore share the phenotype distribution and 883 hits, while hit locations range from nearly random at 1.05×1.05\times mean enrichment to six concentrated clusters at 17.71×17.71\times. Surrogates receive only candidate coordinates and measured phenotypes.

Screening settings. We use n0=128n_{0}=128, B=32B=32, and T=60T=60, giving a total query budget of 2,048. Each landscape setting has five paired repetitions with independent noise and selection seeds 5–9. Methods share the landscape, initial set, and budget within each repetition. The 17.71×17.71\times landscape contains no noise, so only selection seeds vary in this setting. Model and training settings follow the real tasks. TDAL and PoH retain their empirical hit frequency and Gaussian tail estimators, respectively.

The comparison includes TDAL and the eleven baselines in Figure 4, giving 300 runs across five settings. Their mean hit enrichments are 1.051.05, 2.532.53, 3.833.83, 10.0010.00, and 17.71×17.71\times. Enrichment is computed using ten nearest neighbors in the full pool with Euclidean distances in the fixed coordinates, then averaged over the five realizations. The four snapshots in Figure 4b show the first realization with its own enrichment. Table E2 reports final recall for these same methods and settings, and Figure E1 shows their discovery trajectories.

Discovery performance. With nearly random hit locations, mean discovery gains are close to one. Between the least and most clustered settings, TDAL’s mean gain over Random rises from 1.04×1.04\times to 2.26×2.26\times, and PoH’s from 1.06×1.06\times to 1.94×1.94\times. OAE, UCB, and TS reach gains of 1.62×1.62\times, 1.62×1.62\times, and 1.67×1.67\times, respectively, at the highest enrichment. Thus, clustered hits provide useful information for several acquisition functions, although their gains differ across settings. BADGE and KMeans-Embedding do not improve consistently with clustering, while EI, TopUncertain, and DiscoBAX remain below Random in the four structured settings.

Appendix F Ablation Studies and Selection Dynamics

F.1  Component Ablations

We compare five ablations with full TDAL on IFN-γ\gamma, IL-2, Kuzmin, and Horlbeck Jurkat. All methods share the surrogate configuration, fixed candidate representations, initial sets, experimental budgets, and five random seeds. Final cumulative hit counts are reported in Table 1.

Surrogate only. This ablation refits the same surrogate as TDAL after each round of observations but selects candidates with the highest p^t​(x)\hat{p}_{t}(x) without training an acquisition network, breaking exact probability ties at random. Its mean final recall is 0.54–13.01 percentage points lower than full TDAL across the four tasks. Updating response predictions alone therefore does not recover the full model’s discovery gains. Learning a selection function from batch feedback further improves screening.

w/o adaptive wtw_{t}. This ablation retains successor value bootstrapping but replaces the adaptive Hellinger weight with 1, applying the same successor weight in every round. Mean final recall decreases by 3.88–9.03 percentage points across the four tasks. Giving successor value full weight at every round therefore performs less well than adjusting its contribution to the observed prediction changes.

w/o LBO. This ablation disables LBO transitions constructed from the initial set, the associated initial TD training, and online LBO. The acquisition network learns only after receiving real batch feedback. Mean final recall is 0.42–5.54 percentage points lower than full TDAL across the four tasks. LBO reuses measured outcomes to provide training experience at initialization and supplement the single real transition obtained per online round.

w/o successor. This ablation sets the training target to Y=RY=R, retaining the hit probability term, acquisition network, and both real and LBO transitions. With surrogate predictions held fixed, the network fits the difference between the observed batch discovery count and its surrogate estimate. Mean final recall exceeds Surrogate only on all four tasks but is 0.15–1.21 percentage points lower than full TDAL. Current feedback can therefore train an effective selection function, while successor value bootstrapping further increases final discoveries.

w/o anchor. This ablation uses qθ​(st,x)=fθ​(st,ct​(x))q_{\theta}(s_{t},x)=f_{\theta}(s_{t},c_{t}(x)). Both current and successor batch values sum network outputs without explicitly adding p^t​(x)\hat{p}_{t}(x). Surrogate prediction features remain in the inputs. Relative to full TDAL, mean final recall decreases by 0.96 and 2.82 percentage points on IFN-γ\gamma and IL-2, respectively, and increases by 0.31 and 0.16 points on Kuzmin and Horlbeck Jurkat. The two single perturbation tasks each use 60 screening rounds, whereas the two combinatorial tasks each use 200. More rounds provide the acquisition network with more feedback and training opportunities. The explicit hit probability term is more beneficial on the two tasks with 60 rounds. This pattern is consistent with a useful probability reference early in learning and motivates gradually reducing its contribution as feedback accumulates. Testing such a schedule within the same task would separate the effect of screening horizon from differences between datasets.

F.2  Training Dynamics and Candidate Reranking

Candidates analyzed. On IL-2, 85 hit candidates are discovered during active screening in all five TDAL runs and none of the five Surrogate only runs. We compare their discovery times and selection ranks across the five random seeds.

Training and discovery across seeds. Figure F1a–b shows TD loss per round and cumulative discoveries among these 85 candidates. Early loss changes vary in direction and magnitude across seeds. For all five seeds, fluctuations are smaller in the last 30 than in the first 10 rounds. Discoveries concentrate in the second half, with 74.1%–87.1% of the set discovered in the last 30 rounds (Table F1). This common timing pattern shows that these candidates mostly enter selected batches after feedback accumulates.

Candidate reranking at selection. We compare each candidate’s TDAL score rank and concurrent surrogate hit probability rank at selection, using the same unmeasured pool and surrogate predictions. Across seeds, mean TDAL ranks are 16.1–17.2, whereas mean surrogate ranks are 9,442–9,780. Of 425 selection records, 413 have surrogate ranks outside the top B=32B=32 (97.2%, Figure F1c–g). Across seeds, the acquisition network consistently promotes candidates ranked low by concurrent surrogate predictions into the selected batch.

Appendix G Batch Size Sensitivity and Computational Cost

G.1  Batch Size Sensitivity

Experimental settings. We vary batch size at fixed initial sample size and query budget on IL-2 and Simpson K562 to compare discovery at different feedback frequencies. IL-2 uses n0=128n_{0}=128, M=2,048M=2{,}048, and B∈{16,32,64,128}B\in\{16,32,64,128\}. Simpson K562 uses n0=1,024n_{0}=1{,}024, M=26,624M=26{,}624, and B∈{64,128,256,512}B\in\{64,128,256,512\}. Tables G1–G2 give the corresponding numbers of rounds. TDAL, PoH, UCB, BADGE, and CoreSet retain their respective model and training hyperparameters and share the candidate pool, initial set, and budget within each task and seed. Each setting uses five seeds.

Single perturbations. On IL-2, TDAL has the highest mean at B=16,32,64B=16,32,64. At B=128B=128, TDAL’s mean decreases to 252.2 with greater variation across seeds, while PoH reaches 351.4. This setting provides only 15 rounds of experimental feedback and no initial LBO, illustrating performance under limited training experience.

Double perturbations. On Simpson K562, TDAL stays in the top two at all four batch sizes, close to PoH. TDAL has the highest means at B=64,256B=64,256, while PoH is slightly higher at B=128,512B=128,512. TDAL’s mean declines with larger batches, remaining above UCB, BADGE, and CoreSet. At a fixed query budget, larger batches leave fewer rounds for incorporating experimental feedback and training the acquisition function. Smaller batches provide more opportunities to update selection, while PoH remains competitive at larger batches.

G.2  Computational Cost

On IL-2, we use n0=128n_{0}=128, B=32B=32, and the full budget M=2,048M=2{,}048, measuring active rounds 2–4 for each method with seeds 0–2. Each run has exclusive access to one NVIDIA A800 80 GB GPU and eight CPU cores, with runs for different seeds executed sequentially. Mean time per round excludes initialization and the first round, and includes selection and all model updates within the measured rounds. Peak host memory and reserved GPU memory are recorded over the same window, including persistent model and replay state.

TDAL achieves 42.08% final recall on IL-2, with a mean time of 7.40 seconds per round, 1.12 GiB peak host memory, and 0.051 GiB peak reserved GPU memory (Figure G1). DiscoBAX takes 157.78 seconds per round, 21.3 times the TDAL runtime, and reserves 2.674 GiB of GPU memory.
